source.title: Anabasis
source.attribution: Xenophon, Anabasis (trans. H. G. Dakyns), Project Gutenberg, public domain

cards.title: Cyrus the Younger turned a brush with death into a plan to seize the throne
cards.body:
In 404 BC the Persian king Darius II died and his elder son Artaxerxes took the crown. Xenophon tells how a governor named Tissaphernes accused the younger son, Cyrus, of plotting, and Artaxerxes arrested him. Only their mother's pleading saved his life and sent him back to his province around Sardis, in what is now western Turkey.

Cyrus came away from that humiliation determined never to be in his brother's power again, and then to replace him. Quietly he won over visitors, trained his troops and began hiring Greek soldiers.

A wound to pride can drive a whole life. It helps to notice when a big plan is really an answer to an old hurt.
cards.quote: He then, having so escaped through peril and dishonour, fell to considering, not only how he might avoid ever again being in his brother's power, but how, if possible, he might become king in his stead.
cards.apply_it: Think of one ambition you hold strongly. Ask honestly: is any part of it an answer to an old slight?

quiz.question: What set Cyrus on the road to rebellion, according to Xenophon?
options: His father ordered him to take the throne
His brother had him arrested and nearly killed
The Greeks begged him to lead them
quiz.explanation: After Tissaphernes slandered him, Artaxerxes arrested Cyrus; their mother saved him, and he resolved to become king himself.

cards.title: Soldiers hired under a cover story stopped marching when they guessed the truth
cards.body:
Cyrus gathered his Greek mercenaries in 401 BC on a false pretext: a punishing raid on the Pisidians, a hill people of southern Turkey. Only Clearchus, the Spartan exile at the heart of the plan, knew the real target was the king himself.

By the time the army reached Tarsus, in southern Turkey, the men had worked it out. They refused to go on and stayed put for twenty days. When Clearchus tried to force them forward, they threw stones at him and he barely escaped.

People can be led a long way without the full story, but the moment they discover it, trust snaps. If you need commitment to a hard goal, name the goal.
cards.quote: refusing to advance further, since the suspicion ripened in their minds, that the expedition was in reality directed against the king
cards.apply_it: Is there a goal you are steering people toward without saying so? Consider telling them plainly this week.

quiz.question: Why did the Greek soldiers halt at Tarsus?
options: They had not been paid at all
Winter had closed the mountain passes
They suspected the march was really against the Persian king
quiz.explanation: They had signed up for a campaign against the Pisidians and grew suspicious that the true target was Artaxerxes.

cards.title: Clearchus won back his mutinous men with tears and a promise to share their fate
cards.body:
After his soldiers stoned him at Tarsus, Clearchus changed tactics. He called an assembly and stood weeping in silence before he spoke. Cyrus had been his benefactor, he said, but if forced to choose, he would choose his men and go wherever they went.

It worked: more than two thousand soldiers from other units joined him. Yet Xenophon adds that Clearchus was secretly sending word to Cyrus not to worry, since all would turn out right. The emotional speech was partly a move in a longer game.

A moving appeal is not proof of sincerity. When someone's feelings sway you, also look at what they are doing out of sight.
cards.quote: Whether I am about to do right or not, I cannot say, but I choose yourselves; and, whatever betide, I mean to share your fate.
cards.apply_it: Next time a speech moves you to act, wait a day and check the speaker's actions before deciding.

quiz.question: What was Clearchus doing in secret while he told his men he had chosen them over Cyrus?
options: Sending messages telling Cyrus all would come right
Planning to desert to the king
Hiring a ship to sail home
quiz.explanation: Xenophon reports that Clearchus privately told Cyrus to keep a good heart, because things would work out.

cards.title: Cyrus bet that a fast march could beat an empire's size
cards.body:
Through the summer of 401 BC Cyrus drove his army down the Euphrates, across the desert of what is now Syria and Iraq, stopping only for supplies. Xenophon explains his reasoning: the faster he moved, the less time the king had to gather troops.

Xenophon adds a sharp observation. The Persian empire looked mighty because of its vast land and people, but that same size was a weakness. Its roads were long and its forces scattered, so an invader who pressed on quickly could reach the heart before the defence came together.

Small teams facing big rivals can use the same idea. Size brings slowness; speed and focus can matter more than numbers.
cards.quote: being convinced that the more rapidly he advanced, the less prepared for battle would he find the king; while the slower his own progress, the larger would be the hostile army which he would find collected.
cards.apply_it: Where are you competing with someone bigger? Name one thing you can do faster than they can.

quiz.question: What weakness did Xenophon see in the Persian empire's great size?
options: Long roads and scattered forces made it slow to respond
quiz.explanation: The empire's extent meant long distances and dispersed defences, which a fast-moving invader could exploit.

cards.title: At Cunaxa, Clearchus guarded his own flank instead of striking the king
cards.body:
The armies met at Cunaxa, on the Euphrates north of Babylon in modern Iraq, in 401 BC. Xenophon passes on reports of an enormous royal army; modern historians think his figures far too high, but Cyrus was certainly outnumbered.

Cyrus rode up and told Clearchus to attack the centre, where the king stood: hit there and the war was won. But the king's line was so long that his centre lay beyond the Greek left. Clearchus, afraid of being surrounded, kept his right wing anchored on the river and only promised that all would go well.

The Greeks routed the troops in front of them. The decisive point was elsewhere. Winning your own corner is not the same as winning.
cards.quote: 'And if we strike home at this point,' he added, 'our work is finished.'
cards.apply_it: List your tasks for today. Which one, if done, would make most of the others unnecessary? Start there.

quiz.question: Why did Clearchus not lead the Greeks against the king's centre?
options: He had secretly joined the king
He feared being outflanked if he left the river
Cyrus told him to stay put
quiz.explanation: He was afraid of being turned on both flanks and kept his wing on the Euphrates.

cards.title: Cyrus died rushing at his brother at the very moment his side seemed to be winning
cards.body:
While the Greeks chased the enemy off their part of the field, Cyrus held back his six hundred horsemen to watch the king. When Artaxerxes began to wheel round, Cyrus charged, broke the guard and scattered them. But his own riders scattered in pursuit, leaving him with a handful of friends.

Then he saw his brother. Xenophon, drawing on the court doctor Ctesias, says Cyrus cried out, struck the king and wounded him, and was himself killed by a javelin under the eye. His head and right hand were cut off. His cause died with him.

The moment of near victory is dangerous. Impatience then can undo everything that patience built.
cards.quote: Unable longer to contain himself, with a cry, 'I see the man,' he rushed at him and dealt a blow at his chest, wounding him through the corselet.
cards.apply_it: When something you want is suddenly within reach, pause for one breath and ask what you are leaving unprotected.

quiz.question: What left Cyrus almost alone when he reached the king?
options: His own horsemen scattered in pursuit of the enemy
His Greek allies refused to follow
He had sent his guard to protect the camp
quiz.explanation: After routing the king's guard, his six hundred riders broke away to chase them, leaving him with a few companions.

cards.title: Xenophon said Cyrus's power rested on one habit: he kept his word
cards.body:
After the battle, Xenophon wrote a portrait of the dead prince. Whatever else he was, Cyrus kept every treaty and promise. Cities chose to come under him rather than Tissaphernes because an agreement with Cyrus could be trusted, even by enemies.

Xenophon also notes that Cyrus punished wrongdoers harshly, with mutilations by the roadside, and that his generosity was aimed at winning loyalty. He was no saint. But people across the empire crossed over to serve him, and his friends died fighting beside him.

Reliability compounds. People will stake a great deal on someone whose word holds, which is why a broken promise costs far more than it seems.
cards.quote: He would tell no lies to any one.
cards.apply_it: Think of a small promise you have let slide. Keep it today, or tell the person honestly you can't.

quiz.question: Why, according to Xenophon, did cities prefer Cyrus to Tissaphernes?
options: Cyrus's treaties and promises could be relied on
quiz.explanation: Xenophon stresses that Cyrus faithfully kept every compact, so even former enemies trusted his terms.

cards.title: When the king demanded their weapons, the Greeks refused to give up their only leverage
cards.body:
The morning after Cunaxa the Greeks learned Cyrus was dead. Heralds from Artaxerxes arrived with a message: the king had won, so hand over your arms and come and beg for terms.

The generals answered one by one. Clearchus said conquerors do not usually give up their arms. A young Athenian put it most clearly: all they had left were weapons and courage, and without the first the second was useless. Later Clearchus added that whether they were to be friends or enemies of the king, they were worth more armed.

In any negotiation, notice what gives you standing. Giving it away to look agreeable rarely buys the goodwill you hoped for.
cards.quote: If we keep the former we imagine we can make use of the latter; but if we deliver up our arms we shall presently be robbed of our lives.
cards.apply_it: Before your next negotiation, write down the one thing you must not give up, and why.

quiz.question: What did the young Athenian argue about keeping their weapons?
options: Weapons could be sold for food
Without arms, their courage was useless and their lives at risk
The king would respect them more unarmed
quiz.explanation: He said their arms and valour were all they had; surrendering the arms meant losing their lives.

cards.title: The Greek generals walked into a dinner invitation and never came back
cards.body:
For weeks the Greeks marched north with Tissaphernes, each side watching the other. By the Greater Zab river in northern Iraq, Clearchus went to talk the suspicion out. He came back charmed, convinced Tissaphernes was a friend, and insisted the generals and captains go to his tent together to name the slanderers.

Some soldiers objected that it was unwise for all the leaders to go. Clearchus overruled them. Five generals and twenty captains went. At a signal the generals were seized and the captains killed; the generals were later beheaded at the king's court.

Never put everyone you depend on in one place at the mercy of someone you are unsure of. Listen to the doubters, even when you feel certain.
cards.quote: Some of the soldiers protested: the captains and generals had better not all go; it was better not to put too much confidence in Tissaphernes.
cards.apply_it: Where do you have a single point of failure, at work or at home? Add one backup this week.

quiz.question: What warning did some soldiers give before the generals went to Tissaphernes?
options: That not all the leaders should go, and he should not be trusted too far
That he had no food to offer
That the king had already left
quiz.explanation: They protested that the generals and captains should not all go and that Tissaphernes deserved little trust.

cards.title: Clearchus ruled by fear, and his men left him as soon as danger passed
cards.body:
Xenophon's portrait of Clearchus, the Spartan who died at about fifty, is frank. He loved war so much he chose it over peace and wealth. In danger he kept his head, and he was brilliant at finding supplies.

His method was severity. He scowled, shouted and punished so harshly he sometimes regretted it, and he believed a soldier must fear his commander more than the enemy. In a crisis the men wanted no one else. But once the danger was over, many transferred to other officers. They felt toward him as schoolboys to a strict master.

Fear can get results in an emergency. It rarely earns loyalty that lasts beyond it.
cards.quote: But when the pinch of danger was past, and it was open to them to go and taste subordination under some other officer, many forsook him.
cards.apply_it: Think of a leader you obeyed out of fear. What would have made you follow them by choice?

quiz.question: How did soldiers treat Clearchus once a crisis had passed?
options: They held a feast in his honour
Many left to serve under other officers
They demanded he lead them home
quiz.explanation: In danger they wanted him above all, but afterwards many forsook him for gentler commanders.

cards.title: Proxenus was honest and kind, but he feared his soldiers more than they respected him
cards.body:
Proxenus of Thebes, Xenophon's friend, was thirty when he was killed. He had studied under the famous teacher Gorgias and longed to do great things, but only by fair means: he would rather give up a goal than win it dishonestly.

His weakness was the opposite of Clearchus's. He could lead decent people well, but he could not make himself respected or feared. He worried more about his men's dislike than they did about his opinion. Good soldiers loved him; bad ones saw him as someone they could handle.

Kindness is a strength, but leading also means being willing to be unpopular. Without that, the least considerate people end up setting the terms.
cards.quote: he was indisputably more apprehensive of incurring their hatred than they were of losing their fidelity.
cards.apply_it: Is there a boundary you avoid enforcing because you fear being disliked? Decide how you will hold it, kindly but firmly.

quiz.question: What was Proxenus's main weakness as a commander?
options: He feared being disliked and failed to command respect
He was too harsh with punishments
quiz.explanation: Xenophon says he cared more about his men's goodwill than they cared about his, so the unruly took advantage.

cards.title: Menon thought honesty was for fools, and Xenophon shows where that led
cards.body:
The third portrait is of Menon the Thessalian, a young commander Xenophon plainly despised. He wanted wealth above all, and sought power and powerful friends only as tools for it. Lies, false oaths and cheating were, to him, simply the quickest route; honest people were weaklings to exploit.

He was suspected of feeding Tissaphernes slanders against Clearchus. When the other generals were seized, he alone was spared at first. Xenophon reports he was later put to death after a year of suffering and disgrace.

Some people treat your trust as an opening. Watch for anyone who mocks honesty, ridicules friends behind their backs or keeps winning favour by running others down.
cards.quote: for in his vocabulary simplicity and truth were synonyms of folly.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone who often runs down people close to you. What might they gain from it?

quiz.question: What did Menon regard as foolish, according to Xenophon?
quiz.explanation: Menon counted honesty and plain dealing as folly and prided himself on fraud.

cards.title: The night their generals were taken, the Greeks were too heartbroken to eat or sleep
cards.body:
In autumn 401 BC, more than a thousand miles from home, the Greeks found themselves leaderless. They had no guides and no cavalry, there were rivers in the way, their Persian allies had deserted them, and they were surrounded by a hostile empire.

Xenophon does not hide what that night was like. Few ate or lit a fire. Many did not come back to camp, lying down wherever they happened to be. They could not sleep for longing for their homes, parents, wives and children, whom they did not expect to see again.

Despair is a normal response to a desperate situation, even for tough people. Naming it honestly is often the first step to getting up again.
cards.quote: They could not close their eyes for very pain and yearning after their fatherlands or their parents, the wife or child whom they never expected to look upon again.
cards.apply_it: If you are in a dark stretch, write one honest sentence about how you feel before deciding what to do next.

quiz.question: How did most of the Greeks spend the night after their generals were seized?
options: Unable to eat or sleep, grieving for home
quiz.explanation: Few ate or lit fires, and they lay awake longing for families they feared they would never see again.

cards.title: Socrates scolded Xenophon for asking how to go before asking whether to go
cards.body:
Xenophon was a young Athenian, a pupil of Socrates, when his friend Proxenus invited him to join Cyrus. Socrates suspected Athens would frown on friendship with Cyrus, who had backed Sparta against Athens, and told him to consult the oracle at Delphi.

Xenophon went, but asked Apollo which gods to sacrifice to so that his journey would go well. Socrates told him off: he had decided to go and only asked how, when the real question was whether he should go at all. Since he had asked, Socrates said, he should do as the god directed.

We often seek advice on how to do something we have already chosen. The better question usually comes first.
cards.quote: But he, when he heard, blamed Xenophon that he had not, in the first instance, inquired of the god, whether it were better for him to go or to stay
cards.apply_it: Before your next big decision, write down whether you should do it at all, before you plan how.

quiz.question: What was Socrates' complaint about Xenophon's question to the oracle?
options: He asked about money instead of safety
He went to the wrong temple
He asked how to make the journey, not whether to make it
quiz.explanation: Xenophon had already settled on going and only asked how to succeed, skipping the more important question.

cards.title: Xenophon held no rank, but he stopped waiting for someone else to act
cards.body:
Xenophon had come along as a guest, not as a general, officer or even soldier. That night he dreamed of a thunderbolt setting his father's house ablaze, and woke with a hard thought. The enemy would come with daylight, and nobody was preparing.

Then he turned the question on himself. Was he waiting for a general to take charge? From which city? Was he waiting to be older? If he gave up now, he would never get older at all.

He got up and called together Proxenus's officers. When everyone is waiting for someone qualified to step forward, sometimes the person who should step forward is you.
cards.quote: I too! what am I waiting for? a general to undertake the work?
cards.apply_it: Name one problem in your group that everyone sees and no one owns. Take the first small step on it today.

quiz.question: What was Xenophon's position in the army before the generals were seized?
options: A guest of Proxenus with no command
quiz.explanation: He had joined at Proxenus's invitation, neither as general, officer nor soldier.

cards.title: Before dawn the army elected new generals, because soldiers take courage from officers
cards.body:
Around midnight, about a hundred surviving officers met in front of the camp. Xenophon told them the soldiers' eyes were on them: if they looked beaten, the men would give up; if they were seen preparing, the men would follow.

He urged them to fill the empty commands at once, since nothing good gets done without leaders. The Spartan Cheirisophus backed him, and before first light the officers chose replacements. Xenophon himself was elected in place of his friend Proxenus.

After a shock, groups look first at whoever is in charge. Filling gaps quickly and visibly steadies everyone.
cards.quote: The soldiers outside have their eyes fixed upon you; if they think that you are faint-hearted, they will turn cowards
cards.apply_it: If your team has had bad news, show one visible sign of preparation today: a plan, a meeting, a first task.

quiz.question: Whose place did Xenophon take as general?
quiz.explanation: The officers chose Xenophon to replace his friend Proxenus.

cards.title: Turn people's thoughts from what they may suffer to what they will do
cards.body:
Xenophon had watched the soldiers drag themselves into camp and to their guard posts with no spirit left. He told the officers that, unless something changed, the men would be useless by night or day.

His cure was to shift their attention. Stop thinking about what might be done to them, and start thinking about what they intended to do. Do that, he said, and their spirits would quickly revive.

The same shift helps in any frightening stretch: an illness, a layoff, a crisis at home. Worry about what might happen to you drains energy. Planning your next action gives some of it back.
cards.quote: The thing is to get them to turn their thoughts to what they mean to do, instead of to what they are likely to suffer.
cards.apply_it: Write down your biggest current worry, then underneath it one action you mean to take about it.

quiz.question: How did Xenophon propose to revive the soldiers' spirits?
options: Let them rest for a week
Turn their thoughts to what they would do rather than what they might suffer
Hide the bad news from them
quiz.explanation: He believed shifting attention from feared suffering to planned action would quickly restore morale.

cards.title: Burn the wagons so the baggage stops being your general
cards.body:
At dawn Xenophon addressed the whole army. His first practical proposal was blunt: burn the wagons and the tents, and throw out everything not needed for fighting, eating or drinking.

His reason was freedom of movement. Wagons decided where an army could go and how fast. Fewer porters meant more men under arms. And if they lost, their goods would be lost anyway. The soldiers agreed, shared out what each needed and threw the rest on the fire.

Possessions, commitments and old projects can quietly start steering your life. Clearing them out lets your real priorities lead again.
cards.quote: The first thing which I recommend is to burn the wagons we have got, so that we may be free to march wherever the army needs, and not, practically, make our baggage train our general.
cards.apply_it: Pick one commitment or object that is steering your choices more than it should. Drop it or schedule its end.

quiz.question: What did Xenophon mean by not making 'our baggage train our general'?
options: Heavy baggage would dictate where and how fast they could go
The baggage held the generals' treasure
The wagons should lead the march
quiz.explanation: Wagons limited the route and pace, so burning them freed the army to go where it needed.

cards.title: Persia removed the leaders to cause chaos; Xenophon promised ten thousand Clearchuses
cards.body:
Xenophon pointed out why the Persians had seized the generals before attacking. While the Greeks had leaders and obeyed them, they were too strong to fight. Persia expected the loss of command to bring confusion and collapse.

So the answer was the opposite. New officers must be more watchful than the old, and every soldier more orderly than before. Anyone standing by should help an officer deal with someone who broke ranks. Then the enemy would face ten thousand Clearchuses, not one. The army voted for it.

A group is strongest when discipline lives in everyone, not just at the top. Then losing one leader does not lose the whole.
cards.quote: So the enemy will be mightily deceived; for on this day they will behold ten thousand Clearchuses instead of one, who will not suffer one man to play the coward.
cards.apply_it: Ask yourself: if your manager vanished tomorrow, which of their standards would you keep up on your own?

quiz.question: Why, according to Xenophon, had the Persians seized the generals first?
options: The generals had insulted the king
They expected leaderless Greeks to fall into confusion
quiz.explanation: The Persians believed confusion and anarchy without leaders would be fatal to the Greeks.

cards.title: Xenophon ended his plan by inviting anyone, even a private soldier, to propose better
cards.body:
Xenophon's dawn speech set out a full plan, but he closed by handing it to the assembly. If anyone had a better idea, even the lowest-ranked soldier, he should speak up. Their safety belonged to all of them.

This was typical of the march. The army was a travelling Greek city: decisions about routes, discipline and strategy were argued out and settled by a show of hands. Cheirisophus called the vote, and every hand went up.

People back a plan more fully when they have had a real chance to change it. Inviting challenge, especially from those with least status, catches mistakes and builds commitment.
cards.quote: Let those who are in favour of these proposals confirm them with all speed, that they may be realised in fact; or if any other course seem better, let not any one, even though he be a private soldier, shrink from proposing it.
cards.apply_it: In your next meeting, explicitly ask the most junior person present whether they see a better way.

quiz.question: How were Xenophon's proposals adopted?
options: By a show of hands in the assembly
quiz.explanation: Cheirisophus put them to the vote and all the soldiers raised their hands.

cards.title: Xenophon admitted his charge was a mistake and turned it into a fix
cards.body:
On the first day of the retreat, Persian archers and slingers hit the Greek rearguard from beyond range. Xenophon led a charge, caught no one, and got his men into trouble falling back.

That evening the older generals blamed him. He agreed they were right; the result proved it. Then he used the failure to define what was missing: slingers who could outrange the enemy and some horsemen. The army found Rhodians who could sling lead shot, offered rewards for volunteers, and by the next day had two hundred slingers and fifty riders.

Owning a mistake quickly frees you to learn from it. Defending it wastes the lesson.
cards.quote: Xenophon admitted that they were right in blaming him: no better proof of that was wanted than the result.
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent mistake. Say plainly what went wrong, then name one concrete fix.

quiz.question: What did Xenophon do after being criticised for his failed charge?
options: Admitted the fault and proposed raising slingers and cavalry
quiz.explanation: He accepted the criticism and used the lesson to recruit slingers and form a small cavalry force.

cards.title: The hollow square broke at every bridge, so the Greeks redesigned it on the march
cards.body:
Moving north along the Tigris, the Greeks marched in a hollow square with baggage in the middle. It kept the non-fighters safe, but it had a flaw. Wherever the road narrowed or a bridge had to be crossed, the sides were squeezed together and men lost their places; when the sides spread out again, gaps opened. Each time, the enemy pounced.

The generals formed six companies of a hundred men, each with its own officers. When the square narrowed, these companies dropped back; when it widened, they filled the gaps.

Structures that work on open ground can fail at the choke points. Build in units that can flex.
cards.quote: And now it was that the Hellenes discovered the defect of marching in a square with an enemy following.
cards.apply_it: Find where your routine breaks down under pressure, and build one flexible fallback for that moment.

quiz.question: What problem did the hollow square have?
options: It got jammed at narrow points and opened gaps when it widened
quiz.explanation: At bridges and narrow roads the wings were crushed together, and when they spread out gaps appeared.

cards.title: When a soldier said 'easy for you on a horse', Xenophon got off and carried his shield
cards.body:
Near the Tigris the Persians raced the Greeks for a summit above the road. Xenophon rode beside his men urging them on. A soldier named Soteridas snapped back that they were not equal: Xenophon was mounted, while he had to haul his shield.

Xenophon jumped down, pushed Soteridas out of the line, took his shield and marched on foot, weighed down by his own cavalry armour too. The other soldiers turned on Soteridas until he took his shield back. The Greeks reached the summit first.

A leader asking for effort is far more convincing when sharing the burden, especially when someone points out that they are not.
cards.quote: In another instant he had pushed Soteridas from the ranks, snatched from him his shield, and begun marching as quickly as he might under the circumstances
cards.apply_it: Next time you ask your team for extra effort, take on a visible share of the hard part yourself.

quiz.question: How did the other soldiers react to Soteridas's complaint?
options: They pelted and abused him until he took back his shield
quiz.explanation: Seeing Xenophon carry the shield, the men turned on Soteridas until he resumed his load.

cards.title: The generals questioned prisoners about every route without revealing their choice
cards.body:
Hemmed in by the Tigris, which was too deep to ford, and by high mountains, the Greeks turned back to unburnt villages and questioned their prisoners. South lay Babylon; east lay the royal capitals; west, across the river, lay Lydia. North, through the mountains, lived the Carduchians, a fiercely independent people of what is now southeastern Turkey, who answered to no king.

The generals sat apart those who claimed to know each route, careful not to show which way they meant to go. Then they chose the mountains, beyond which lay Armenia.

When gathering advice, don't reveal your preferred answer too early. People tend to tell you what they think you want.
cards.quote: they put them to sit apart without making it clear which particular route they intended to take.
cards.apply_it: Next time you ask for opinions, describe the options neutrally before saying which you favour.

quiz.question: Why did the generals keep their chosen route hidden while questioning prisoners?
options: So their intentions would not leak or shape the answers
quiz.explanation: They seated knowledgeable informants apart without making clear which route they intended to take.

cards.title: In the Carduchian mountains the front and rear of the army kept rescuing each other
cards.body:
The march through the Carduchian hills took seven days, probably in late 401 BC, and Xenophon says it was harder than everything the king and Tissaphernes had done to them put together. The mountain people blocked every narrow pass and attacked from above with long bows and boulders.

Cheirisophus led the front and Xenophon the rear. Whenever the front was blocked, Xenophon climbed around to get above the attackers; whenever the rear was hit, Cheirisophus did the same. The two divisions saved each other again and again.

The tough stretches go better when each part of a team watches the other's weak point, and moves without being asked.
cards.quote: and in this way, turn and turn about, they rescued each other, and paid unflinching attention to their mutual needs.
cards.apply_it: Ask a teammate what threatens their work most right now, and offer one concrete way to cover it.

quiz.question: How did Xenophon and Cheirisophus deal with blocked passes in the mountains?
options: They waited for the enemy to leave
Whoever was free climbed round above the attackers to free the other
quiz.explanation: Each took turns outflanking the attackers from higher ground to free the other division.

cards.title: Xenophon could be woken at any hour, so two young soldiers brought him the ford
cards.body:
At the Centrites river, the border of Armenia in modern southeastern Turkey, the Greeks were trapped. The water was chest-deep and fast, an Armenian force held the far bank, and the Carduchians waited behind.

Next morning two young men ran up to Xenophon at breakfast. Collecting firewood, they had seen people hiding bundles in a cave across the river and had waded over without the water reaching their hips. Everyone knew they could come to him, even if he was asleep, with anything about the war. The army crossed that day.

The answer to a stuck problem often sits with someone low down. They will only bring it if they know you are approachable.
cards.quote: for every one knew that, breakfasting or supping, he was always accessible, or that even if asleep any one was welcome to awaken him who had anything to say bearing on the business of war.
cards.apply_it: Tell your team, in words, that they can interrupt you with anything urgent, and thank the first person who does.

quiz.question: How did the Greeks find a way across the Centrites?
options: Two young soldiers spotted a shallow crossing and told Xenophon
quiz.explanation: Two young men collecting firewood waded across, then ran to Xenophon, who was known to be always accessible.

cards.title: In the Armenian snow, the danger was how comfortable it felt to stay lying down
cards.body:
Crossing the Armenian highlands of eastern Turkey in winter, the army camped in the open. During the night snow fell so thickly that it buried the stacked weapons and the sleeping men.

Xenophon notices a strange thing: nobody wanted to get up. The snow lay over them like a warm blanket. Then Xenophon himself rose, without his cloak, and started splitting wood. One man after another got up, took the axe from him and joined in, and soon fires were lit.

The states that harm us most can feel cosy. Often the way out is one person starting a simple task, and others following.
cards.quote: and there was great unreadiness to get up, so gently fell the snow as they lay there warm and comfortable, and formed a blanket, except where it slipped off the sleepers' shoulders
cards.apply_it: When you feel stuck in a comfortable rut, start one simple physical task for five minutes and see who joins you.

quiz.question: What finally got the snowbound soldiers moving?
options: Xenophon getting up and splitting wood
quiz.explanation: Xenophon rose and began chopping wood; one by one the men took over and lit fires.

cards.title: On the winter march men fell to frostbite, snow-blindness and exhaustion
cards.body:
The winter of 401 to 400 BC in the Armenian highlands was brutal. Xenophon describes snow six feet deep and a north wind that numbed everyone. On one stage alone many pack animals and slaves were lost, and about thirty soldiers.

Men collapsed from hunger and revived when given food. Others were left behind, blinded by snow or with toes destroyed by frost. Xenophon records what helped: holding something dark before the eyes against the glare, and for the feet, never stopping, and loosening sandals at night so the straps did not freeze into them.

It is a reminder of the real cost behind famous retreats, and of how simple, practical knowledge can save lives.
cards.quote: for the feet, the only remedy was to keep in motion without stopping for an instant, and to loose the sandal at night.
cards.apply_it: Think of a hardship you came through. Write down one practical lesson from it that could help someone else.

quiz.question: What remedy for frozen feet does Xenophon record?
options: Keeping moving and loosening the sandals at night
Sitting by a fire all day
quiz.explanation: He says the only remedy was to keep moving without stopping and to loosen the sandal at night.

cards.title: When exhausted men refused to move, Xenophon used the one thing they could still do
cards.body:
Some soldiers fell out of the line and sat down by a warm spring in the snow. Xenophon begged them to keep going, warning that the enemy were close. He grew angry. They told him he could cut their throats; they would not move another step.

So he changed approach. As darkness fell, his rearguard leapt out at the pursuing enemy, while the sick men shouted as loudly as they could and banged spears on shields. The pursuers fled in panic. The next day the rearguard sent young men back to get the invalids moving.

When someone is too drained to do what you ask, find the smaller thing they can still do, and let it count.
cards.quote: They merely bade him put a knife to their throats; not one step farther would they stir.
cards.apply_it: If someone you care about is worn out, ask for one small contribution they can manage instead of the whole task.

quiz.question: How did the exhausted soldiers help drive off the enemy?
options: They set the woods on fire
They shouted and clashed their spears against their shields
quiz.explanation: While the rearguard charged, the sick men yelled and banged spears on shields, and the enemy fled.

cards.title: Xenophon treated the village headman as a guest; Cheirisophus struck him and lost him
cards.body:
In an Armenian village the Greeks seized the headman to act as their guide, keeping his son as a hostage. Xenophon had him to supper, promised to leave his house well stocked, and gave him a horse to sacrifice, since he was a priest of the sun. The headman showed them stored food and taught them to wrap sacks around the horses' hooves in snow.

On the road Cheirisophus lost his temper when no villages appeared, hit the headman, and forgot to tie him up. That night the guide ran away. Xenophon called it the only quarrel the two generals had on the whole march.

The people you depend on most are often the easiest to mistreat. Their goodwill is worth guarding.
cards.quote: This was the sole ground of difference between Cheirisophus and Xenophon during the march, this combination of ill-treatment and neglect in the case of the guide.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone whose help you rely on but rarely thank. Thank them specifically today.

quiz.question: What caused the only disagreement between Cheirisophus and Xenophon?
options: Cheirisophus beating and then neglecting the guide, who escaped
quiz.explanation: Xenophon names Cheirisophus's ill-treatment and neglect of the headman as their sole difference.

cards.title: Facing a guarded pass, Xenophon asked how to lose the fewest men, not how to win the fight
cards.body:
Beyond the river Phasis, in northeastern Turkey, local tribes held the pass the Greeks needed. One general wanted to attack straight away. Xenophon reframed the problem: the goal was to cross with the fewest wounds and the fewest good men lost.

The mountain was long and the enemy only guarded the road. Better to slip a force up an unguarded part at night than to storm a prepared position. He even teased the Spartan Cheirisophus that Spartans trained in stealing from boyhood; Cheirisophus joked back about Athenians stealing public money. Volunteers took the heights that night, and the defenders fled.

When a goal looks like a fight, ask what you actually need. Often there is a way round.
cards.quote: if we desire to cross with the greatest ease, the point to consider is, how we may get the fewest wounds and throw away the smallest number of good men.
cards.apply_it: For a conflict you face, write what you really need from it, then list one way to get that without a showdown.

quiz.question: What plan did Xenophon propose for crossing the guarded pass?
options: A full frontal assault at dawn
Slipping a force onto an unguarded part of the mountain at night
quiz.explanation: He argued for seizing an undefended stretch by night rather than attacking a prepared enemy.

cards.title: The retreat that saved the Greeks brought disaster to the people in its path
cards.body:
An army of over ten thousand with no supplies survived by taking food from whoever lived along the route. In the land of the Taochians, in northeastern Turkey, villagers had carried their stores up into strongholds, and the hungry Greeks stormed one.

Xenophon records what followed without flinching: rather than be captured, many of the families inside threw themselves from the cliffs. Hardly any people were taken alive; mostly cattle and sheep.

The Anabasis is often read as a tale of courage and survival, and it is one. It is also a record of what an army on the move cost the communities it passed through. Good history asks how events looked from both sides.
cards.quote: Out of this place the merest handful of human beings were taken prisoners, but cattle and asses in abundance and flocks of sheep.
cards.apply_it: Think of a story you know only from the winners' side. Look up how the other side remembered it.

quiz.question: Why did the Greeks attack the Taochian stronghold?
options: They were starving and the Taochians had stored their food there
quiz.explanation: Provisions had run out, and the Taochians had carried all their stores into fortified places.

cards.title: From a mountaintop the soldiers saw the sea and cried 'The sea! The sea!'
cards.body:
Early in 400 BC a local guide promised to show the army the sea within five days, staking his life on it. On the fifth day the front ranks climbed Mount Theches, in northeastern Turkey near modern Trabzon.

Xenophon, at the rear, heard shouting and assumed an attack. He rode forward with the cavalry and then heard the word being passed back: the sea. The Black Sea meant Greek cities and a way home. Everyone ran to the top, generals and soldiers alike, embracing in tears. They piled up a great cairn of stones and captured shields.

Long struggles need moments of sight: a point where you can see the end. It is worth marking them.
cards.quote: Presently they could hear the soldiers shouting and passing on the joyful word, 'The sea! the sea!'
cards.apply_it: In a long project, identify the next point where you will be able to 'see the sea', and plan how you will mark it.

quiz.question: What did Xenophon first think the shouting from the front meant?
options: That enemies were attacking the vanguard
That the guide had run away
quiz.explanation: He assumed another enemy was attacking the front, until he heard the cry 'The sea! the sea!'

cards.title: A former slave recognised the enemy's language and talked a battle into a truce
cards.body:
Near the coast the Macrones lined up on the far side of a river to stop the Greeks, throwing stones. A light-armed soldier came to Xenophon: he had been a slave in Athens, and he thought he recognised their speech. This might be his homeland.

Xenophon told him to talk to them. The Macrones said they were defending their country. The Greeks replied that they meant no harm and only wanted to reach the sea. The two sides swapped spears as pledges, and the Macrones cut a road through the woods, sold them food and guided them for three days.

Many conflicts end when someone finds a shared language. Ask who in your group can bridge the gap.
cards.quote: 'I think,' said he, 'that this must be my native country, and if there is no objection I will have a talk with them.'
cards.apply_it: In a tense situation, ask the other side plainly why they object, and state plainly what you want.

quiz.question: How did the Greeks and Macrones seal their agreement?
quiz.explanation: The Macrones gave a native lance and the Greeks a Greek lance as pledges, calling the gods to witness.

cards.title: While waiting for promised ships, Xenophon arranged a backup supply of his own
cards.body:
At Trapezus (modern Trabzon) the exhausted soldiers wanted to sail home. Cheirisophus went off to fetch ships from a Spartan admiral he knew, and the army voted to wait.

Xenophon proposed using the wait well: organised foraging, guard posts and, above all, collecting ships locally in case Cheirisophus failed. If he came back with enough, they would simply have extra. When the men shouted down his suggestion of also repairing coastal roads, he didn't force a vote; he quietly persuaded the cities to fix them. Cheirisophus was delayed, and in the end much of the army had to march.

When your plan depends on someone else delivering, build a fallback that costs little if it is never needed.
cards.quote: If he comes and finds us already provided for here, we shall have more ships than we need, that is all; while, if he fails to bring them, we shall have the local supply to fall back upon.
cards.apply_it: For one thing you are waiting on from someone else, set up a simple backup this week.

quiz.question: Why did Xenophon want to collect ships locally?
options: As a fallback in case Cheirisophus failed to bring enough
To sell them to the Persians
quiz.explanation: He reasoned that extra ships cost little, while having none if Cheirisophus failed would be disastrous.

cards.title: At the roll call by the Black Sea, about 8,600 of the Greeks were still alive
cards.body:
At Cerasus on the Black Sea coast the army held a review in 400 BC and counted 8,600 men under arms. Xenophon puts it simply: the rest had died in fighting, in the snow or of disease. He had earlier given the Greek force before Cunaxa as about 12,900.

When the generals divided the offering set aside for the gods, Xenophon had his share made into a gift for Apollo at Delphi. He inscribed it with his own name and that of Proxenus, the friend who had brought him on the expedition and was killed with Clearchus.

Survival stories have a count behind them. Remembering those who did not make it is part of telling the story honestly.
cards.quote: So many had escaped; the rest had perished at the hands of the enemy, or by reason of the snow, or else disease.
cards.apply_it: Is there someone whose part in your story is easily forgotten? Find a small way to honour it.

quiz.question: Whose name did Xenophon inscribe alongside his own on his offering at Delphi?
quiz.explanation: He dedicated the offering in his own name and that of his friend Proxenus, killed with Clearchus.

cards.title: Accused of plotting to trick the army, Xenophon answered with where the sun sets
cards.body:
At Cotyora, on the Black Sea coast, rumours spread that Xenophon had persuaded the generals to ship the army east to the Phasis instead of home. The soldiers were angry, and a mob seemed close.

Xenophon called an assembly before crowds could gather on their own. He didn't attack his accusers. He reminded the men that Greece lay toward the sunset, that the north wind carried ships home, and that one man on one ship could hardly kidnap ten thousand armed soldiers on a hundred.

When a rumour runs hot, plain facts everyone can check for themselves often cool it faster than outrage or counter-accusation.
cards.quote: I presume, sirs, you know where the sun rises and where he sets, and that he who would go to Hellas must needs journey towards the sunset
cards.apply_it: Next time you're misjudged, answer with one fact the other person can check, not with blame.

quiz.question: What did Xenophon do first when he heard the army was angry with him?
options: Called an assembly before crowds could gather on their own
Asked Cheirisophus to speak for him
quiz.explanation: He had the herald summon a meeting at once so the men would not collect of their own accord.

cards.title: After a mob killed envoys, Xenophon warned that 'Shoot him!' was replacing the vote
cards.body:
Xenophon then laid out a darker matter. A captain had raided a friendly hill village for private gain and died in the attempt. When elders came to talk peace, soldiers stoned them to death. Later a mob chased a market official, and frightened local Greeks leapt into the sea, where some drowned.

Xenophon told the army where this led. Any man with enough followers who shouted 'Shoot him!' could make himself general and kill whoever he liked without trial. No city would trade with them. The assembly ordered ringleaders tried, set up courts of officers and agreed to hold their own generals to account.

A group that lets loud anger replace fair process soon finds itself ruled by its worst members.
cards.quote: any one who likes to elect himself general, and will adopt the formula 'Shoot him! shoot him!' will be competent to cut down whomsoever he pleases untried
cards.apply_it: When a group you belong to gets heated, ask aloud: what is our fair process for deciding this?

quiz.question: What did the army decide after Xenophon's speech on lawlessness?
options: To try the ringleaders and set up courts of officers
quiz.explanation: They resolved that ringleaders be prosecuted, constituted the officers as judges and purified the army.

cards.title: Xenophon stood trial before his own soldiers, and explained why he had struck a man
cards.body:
The army also audited its generals. Some were fined over missing cargo. Xenophon was charged with assault by men he had hit during the winter march.

He questioned the first accuser and the story came out. In the snow Xenophon had ordered this man to carry a sick comrade. Later he found him digging a grave for the man, who then moved his leg. The accuser had said he wouldn't carry him, dead or alive. Xenophon admitted he struck him then. The crowd sided with Xenophon.

Today we would not defend hitting anyone. But the deeper lessons stand: leaders should answer for their conduct in public, and no one should be abandoned for convenience.
cards.quote: 'Nay,' retorted Xenophon, 'by the same token we shall all one day be dead, but that is no reason why meantime we should all be buried alive?'
cards.apply_it: Invite honest feedback on one decision you made as a leader or parent, and listen without defending yourself first.

quiz.question: Why had Xenophon struck the soldier who accused him?
options: He was about to bury a sick comrade who was still alive
He refused to share his wine
quiz.explanation: The man was digging a grave for the comrade he'd been ordered to carry, and refused to carry him alive or dead.

cards.title: Xenophon asked his men why they remembered every blow and none of the help
cards.body:
At the end of his defence, Xenophon turned the question back on the assembly. They remembered keenly each time he had angered someone. But the times he had eased the winter for them, driven off an enemy, cared for the sick or praised a brave act, nobody mentioned.

It would be fairer and kinder, he said, to keep the memory of good rather than of evil. One after another, soldiers stood up to recall the good things, and the meeting ended on a better note.

Our minds hold on to grievances more easily than kindnesses. Deliberately recalling the good someone has done can repair a relationship that a list of complaints would end.
cards.quote: Yet it were surely more noble, just, and holy, sweeter and kindlier to treasure the memory of good rather than of evil.
cards.apply_it: Think of someone you're annoyed with. Write down three good things they have done for you.

quiz.question: What happened after Xenophon asked the soldiers to remember the good as well as the bad?
options: Soldiers stood up to recall good things he had done
The meeting broke up in anger
quiz.explanation: One after another men recalled such incidents, and things ended not so unpleasantly after all.

cards.title: Offered sole command, Xenophon refused, and promised to back whoever was chosen
cards.body:
Near Sinope the army decided one general would act faster than a committee, and the officers pressed Xenophon to take it. He was tempted; it would bring fame. But he also saw that the future was uncertain and he might lose the reputation he had. When he made his sacrifices, the signs he read told him to refuse.

He also argued that choosing an Athenian over a Spartan would anger Sparta, then the most powerful state in Greece. Above all, he promised not to stir up opposition to whoever was chosen. The army elected Cheirisophus.

Not every honour is worth taking. Supporting another leader wholeheartedly can serve a group better than winning the top job.
cards.quote: I hold that whosoever sets up factious opposition to his leader factiously opposes his own safety.
cards.apply_it: Is there someone leading a project you wanted to lead? Find one way to help them succeed this week.

quiz.question: What reason did Xenophon give the army for declining the sole command?
options: Choosing an Athenian over a Spartan could turn Sparta against them
quiz.explanation: He said preferring an Athenian in a Spartan's presence would make it harder to get help from Sparta later.

cards.title: The army split into three, and the breakaway group soon needed rescuing
cards.body:
Within a week of Cheirisophus's election, at Heraclea on the Black Sea coast, the soldiers argued over money. The Arcadians and Achaeans, the largest group, said it was outrageous for an Athenian and a Spartan to command Peloponnesians, and they left to choose ten generals of their own.

The army became three divisions. The breakaway group landed at Calpe Haven, raided villages and was soon surrounded on a hill by Thracian fighters, cut off from water. Xenophon, reasoning that their destruction would doom everyone, marched to their aid; the besiegers slipped away. When the groups met at Calpe, they embraced like brothers.

Splits usually feel like freedom at first. The shared risks remain.
cards.quote: Thus the absolute authority vested in Cheirisophus was terminated there and then, within less than a week of his appointment.
cards.apply_it: If you've drifted from a group you once relied on, consider what risks you still share, and reach out.

quiz.question: Why did the Arcadians and Achaeans break away?
options: They resented being led by an Athenian and a Spartan
They wanted to settle in Asia
quiz.explanation: They argued that the largest contingent should not be ruled by an Athenian and a Spartan who brought no troops.

cards.title: At Byzantium Xenophon calmed a raging army by asking it to fall into ranks
cards.body:
In 400 BC the army crossed to Byzantium, modern Istanbul. The Spartan admiral, who had promised pay, ordered them out of the city without it. Furious, the soldiers burst back through the gates, and the townspeople fled, sure the city was taken.

The men crowded around Xenophon: here was a city, ships, money; he could make them all great. He seemed to agree, but told them first to form ranks. Once they stood in order and tempers cooled, he spoke. Seizing a Greek city would set every Greek state against them, including their own families. They sent a message instead, and marched out.

You can't argue with a mob. You can first help it become an orderly group, and then talk.
cards.quote: 'Nay, I like what you say, and I will do it all; but if that is what you have set your hearts on, fall into rank and take up position at once.'
cards.apply_it: When someone is furious, help them do one calming, ordinary thing (sit down, get water) before discussing the issue.

quiz.question: Why did Xenophon tell the angry soldiers to fall into rank first?
options: To count how many had deserted
To quiet them before reasoning with them
quiz.explanation: He said it wishing to calm them; once the men were formed up and cooler, he called an assembly.

cards.title: Cheated by an ally, Xenophon said the shame belongs to the friend who deceives
cards.body:
That winter the remaining army served Seuthes, a Thracian prince in what is now European Turkey and Bulgaria, in return for promised pay. They won his wars, but he paid only part. The soldiers blamed Xenophon, and some even threatened him.

In his defence he asked whether he should be ashamed of being fooled. If an open enemy had tricked him, yes. But when a friend cheats a friend, he said, the deeper stain falls on the deceiver. They had dealt honestly, worked hard and given Seuthes no excuse.

If someone you trusted has let you down, being trusting is not your failing. The shame of broken faith rests with the one who broke it.
cards.quote: But, to my mind, when friend cheats friend, a deeper stain attaches to the perpetrator than to the victim of deceit.
cards.apply_it: If a betrayal still stings, write one sentence placing the responsibility where it belongs, then set it down.

quiz.question: According to Xenophon, who carries the greater shame when a friend deceives a friend?
quiz.explanation: He argued the deeper stain attaches to the perpetrator rather than the victim.

cards.title: Xenophon came home from leading the Ten Thousand so poor he had to sell his horse
cards.body:
In spring 399 BC the survivors joined a Spartan army under Thibron, fighting the Persian governors in western Turkey. At Lampsacus on the Dardanelles a soothsayer friend asked Xenophon how much gold he had made. Barely enough to get home, he admitted, unless he sold his horse.

The friend didn't believe him until he saw the sacrifice. Xenophon sold the horse. Soon after, two visitors who heard he was fond of it bought it back for him and refused any payment. Later he did profit from a raid, and for many years afterwards he lived on an estate at Scillus in Greece.

Leading well does not always pay well. Sometimes the reward comes as friends who notice what you gave up.
cards.quote: 'Upon my word, I shall have barely enough to get home, unless I sell my horse, and what I have about my person.'
cards.apply_it: Think of something you did that cost you more than it paid. Who noticed? Thank them.

quiz.question: What did Bion and Nausicleides do for Xenophon at the end?
options: Bought back the horse he had sold and returned it
quiz.explanation: Suspecting he had sold it out of need and knowing he loved it, they repurchased the horse and gave it back.
